column3: Trick number two. When the bad news gets in anyway, argue with it.
In a classic study, students were tested for a made up health condition, with a little spit on a strip of paper.
Some were told that if the strip didn't change color, that was bad news. It meant they had the condition.
What they didn't know: the strip was plain yellow paper. It never changed for anyone.
So everyone saw the same thing. Nothing. But not everyone took it the same way.
The bad news group took about thirty seconds longer to decide the test was done. As if the paper just needed more time.
Over half of them retested. Some dipped the strip up to twelve times. In the good news group, under one in five did.
The bad news group also rated the test as less accurate.
Psychologists call this motivated skepticism. Good news, we accept at face value. Bad news has to prove itself.
And notice: nobody here told an outright lie. They just set the bar higher for the answer they didn't want.
